title: Same cards, different work
hook: Five cards, one method. Why does one hand take 10 slides and another none?

knows: ordering numbers from smallest to largest
sorting a hand of playing cards informally
doesNotKnow: that sorting effort depends on how scrambled the input is

misconception: Sorting always costs the same effort for the same number of items.
objective: The learner can explain that each slide in insertion sort fixes one out-of-order pair, so a reversed hand of 5 needs 10 slides, a sorted hand needs none, and the work depends on how scrambled the input is.

claims.text: Sorting the reversed hand 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 by insertion takes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 one-place slides.
claims.source: Card k (k = 2..5) must pass all k - 1 cards before it, since they are all larger. Builder ran insertion sort with a swap counter in Node: 54321 -> 10.

claims.text: A hand already in order needs 0 slides.
claims.source: Every new card is already larger than the card to its left, so no swap happens. Builder ran it: 12345 -> 0.

claims.text: Each slide fixes exactly one out-of-order pair, so the number of slides equals the number of out-of-order pairs (inversions).
claims.source: Swapping two adjacent out-of-order items removes exactly one inversion and creates none (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.1; CLRS 3rd ed., Problem 2-4). Builder brute-force checked the four stage hands: 54321: 10 = 10, 31452: 4 = 4, 12354: 1 = 1, 12345: 0 = 0.

claims.text: A reversed hand of 5 has all 10 of its pairs out of order; the nearly sorted hand 1, 2, 3, 5, 4 has 1.
claims.source: 5 cards form 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 pairs; reversed, every pair is out of order. In 12354 only the pair (5, 4) is out of order.

claims.text: For 100 cards, insertion sort needs 4,950 slides on a reversed hand and none on a sorted one.
claims.source: Reversed n items have n(n - 1)/2 inversions: 100 x 99 / 2 = 4,950. Sorted input has 0. CLRS 3rd ed., 2.2 (worst and best case of insertion sort).

claims.text: 1,000 names in reverse order have 499,500 out-of-order pairs; swapping two neighbours in a sorted list makes just 1.
claims.source: n(n - 1)/2 with n = 1,000 gives 499,500. Swapping two adjacent items of a sorted list inverts only that one pair.

recall.question: Insertion sort gets 1,000 names in order except two neighbours swapped. Compared with 1,000 names in reverse order, its work is:
options: About the same: same number of names
Far less: only one pair is out of order
Far more: it must check every name
recall.why: Insertion sort's slides equal the out-of-order pairs. Two swapped neighbours make one such pair, so one slide; reversed makes every pair out of order, 499,500 of them.
